article.title: Survivorship Bias: What Disappeared From Your Dataset?
article.why: A practical bias that affects customer, employee, product, and investment analysis.

paragraphs.en:
Survivorship bias occurs when an analysis focuses on the people, companies, products, or observations that remain visible while overlooking those that disappeared. The surviving cases are often easier to collect, so the resulting dataset can look complete even though an important part of the original population is missing.

A classic intuition comes from studying successful businesses. If we interview only companies that have operated for twenty years, we may conclude that certain strategies are common among durable firms. But failed companies may have used exactly the same strategies. Without observing them, we cannot tell whether the strategy contributed to survival or merely happened to be present among survivors.

Customer analytics has the same risk. Imagine an app comparing this year's spending with last year's spending only for customers who purchased in both years. The comparison may show strong growth. Yet customers who stopped buying have been excluded by construction. The analysis answers a narrow question—how continuing customers changed—not the broader question of how the customer base performed. If management interprets it as overall customer growth, the conclusion becomes too optimistic.

The bias also appears in employee surveys. A company might ask current employees whether onboarding prepared them well, but people who left after a poor experience are no longer available in the internal survey. Product teams may analyze usage among retained users and discover popular features, while ignoring users who churned because those features did not solve their problems. Investment databases can similarly overrepresent funds that still exist if closed or merged funds are removed from historical comparisons.

Avoiding survivorship bias begins with defining the target population before selecting the analytical sample. Ask who was eligible at the starting point, who later disappeared, and why. Where possible, preserve historical records for churned customers, discontinued products, closed stores, or departed employees. Then report retention and exit explicitly rather than silently dropping those observations.

A useful comparison is to create several views. One view can track a fixed starting cohort, another can describe current active users, and a third can examine entrants and exits separately. These views answer different questions and should not be mixed. If missing cases cannot be recovered, state the limitation and avoid generalizing beyond the observed population.

Survivorship bias is dangerous because the remaining data often looks clean and convincing. Nothing in a spreadsheet automatically announces that the unsuccessful cases have vanished. The analyst has to reconstruct the population history. Before celebrating a pattern among winners, retained customers, or long-lived products, ask a simple question: who had to disappear for this dataset to look this good?

A second safeguard is to compare denominators across reports. If last year's analysis began with 100,000 eligible customers but this year's table contains only 70,000 continuing customers, a percentage calculated on the smaller base should not be presented as if it described the original population. Analysts can create a simple population bridge: starting customers, new entrants, retained customers, churned customers, and customers excluded for operational reasons. This bridge makes disappearance visible. It also helps distinguish a real improvement in behavior from an improvement caused by selective retention. In longitudinal analysis, preserving identifiers and eligibility history is therefore not merely a data-engineering convenience; it is part of the statistical design. A clean table is useful only when we can explain how each row entered, remained in, or left the population.
paragraphs.zh: 【重點翻譯】存活者偏差是指分析只關注仍然留在資料中的人、公司、產品或觀測值，卻忽略已經退出、失敗或消失的案例。留下來的案例通常比較容易取得，因此資料表看起來可能十分完整，實際上卻缺少原始母體中的重要部分。以顧客分析為例，如果只比較連續兩年都有購買的顧客，我們得到的是「持續購買顧客的變化」，而不是「整體客群的成長」。已停止購買的顧客在篩選過程中已被排除，若管理層把前者解讀為整體成長，結論就會過度樂觀。實務上應先定義分析起點的目標母體，再追蹤哪些人留下、哪些人流失，以及流失原因。必要時可以分別觀察固定起始客群、目前活躍客群、新加入者與退出者。若去年有十萬名符合條件的顧客，而今年的表只剩七萬名持續購買者，就不能把以七萬人為分母計算的比例當成原始十萬人的整體表現。
paragraphs.ja: 【要点訳】生存者バイアスとは、現在もデータに残っている人、企業、商品、観測値だけに注目し、すでに離脱・失敗・消滅したケースを見落とすことで生じる偏りである。残っているケースは収集しやすいため、表面上は完全なデータに見えても、元の母集団の重要な一部が欠けていることがある。顧客分析で、2年とも購入した顧客だけを比較した場合、分かるのは「継続顧客がどう変化したか」であり、「顧客基盤全体がどう変化したか」ではない。購入をやめた顧客は最初から比較対象から外れているため、この結果を全体の成長と解釈すると過度に楽観的になる。実務では、分析開始時点の対象母集団を先に定義し、継続者、離脱者、新規流入者を明示的に追跡することが重要である。必要に応じて、固定した開始時点の顧客群、現在の利用者、新規顧客、離脱顧客を別々に確認する。

vocabulary.usage: Survivorship bias appears when only cases that remain observable are analyzed.
The analysis may overlook customers who already churned.
Long-lived firms are not automatically evidence of a durable strategy.
Users who churn may be absent from a survey of current users.
A database can overrepresent funds that still exist.
A fixed cohort keeps the starting population stable over time.
Do not generalize from survivors to the original population without evidence.
Report retention together with changes among retained customers.
